content: This is an updated version of the original Cochrane review, first published in 2015. Focal epilepsies arise from a dysfunction of nerve cells localized to a specific region within one cerebral hemisphere. Studies estimate that between 20% and 70% of individuals with focal epilepsy fail to achieve seizure freedom despite optimal pharmacological treatment. For these patients, if the epileptogenic zone can be accurately identified, surgical resection offers the potential for a cure and an associated improvement in quality of life. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the overall outcomes of epilepsy surgery based on evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Secondary objectives included assessing outcomes based on non-randomized evidence and identifying factors associated with postoperative seizure remission. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted on March 11, 2019, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). Eligible studies were RCTs with at least 30 participants, a well-defined population (considering factors such as age, sex, seizure type/frequency, epilepsy duration, etiology, MRI findings, and surgical outcomes), MRI performed in at least 90% of cases, a minimum follow-up duration of one year, and outcomes related to postoperative seizure control. Cohort studies and case series were included in the earlier version of this review. Three pairs of review authors independently screened references for eligibility, assessed study quality and risk of bias, and extracted data. Outcomes were analyzed based on the proportion of participants achieving favorable results, considering the presence or absence of specific prognostic factors. Data were intended to be combined using risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A total of 182 studies, involving 16,855 participants, were identified for this review. Of these, nine were RCTs, including two trials that compared surgery to medical treatment (99 participants in these trials received medical treatment). The risk of bias in these RCTs was either unclear or high. The remaining 173 studies were predominantly retrospective in design. Study quality was assessed using the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) tool, which revealed that most studies provided moderate or weak evidence. For 29 studies reporting multivariate analyses, the Quality in Prognostic Studies (QUIPS) tool was used, and very few studies were found to have a low risk of bias across all domains. Regarding seizure freedom, two RCTs demonstrated that surgery (n = 97) was superior to medical treatment (n = 99). Four RCTs found no statistically significant differences in seizure outcomes when comparing anterior temporal lobectomy (ATL) with or without corpus callosotomy (n = 60), subtemporal versus transsylvian approaches to selective amygdalohippocampectomy (SAH) (n = 47), ATL versus SAH versus parahippocampectomy (n = 43), or 2.5 cm versus 3.5 cm ATL resection (n = 207). One RCT found total hippocampectomy to be superior to partial hippocampectomy (n = 70), while another found ATL to be superior to stereotactic radiosurgery (n = 58). For Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, one RCT showed no significant differences in seizure outcomes between resection of the epileptogenic zone alone and resection combined with corpus callosotomy (n = 43). The evidence from these nine RCTs was judged to be of moderate to very low quality due to limited reporting on trial design and restricted study populations. Among the 16,756 participants who underwent surgical procedures, 10,696 (64%) achieved favorable outcomes, with success rates ranging from 13.5% to 92.5% across studies. However, the quality of data regarding adverse event reporting was found to be very poor. A total of 120 studies examined between one and eight prognostic factors using univariate analysis. Factors associated with better postoperative seizure outcomes included abnormal preoperative MRI findings, absence of intracranial monitoring, complete surgical resection, presence of mesial temporal sclerosis, concordance between preoperative MRI and electroencephalography (EEG), history of febrile seizures, absence of focal cortical dysplasia or malformations of cortical development, presence of a tumor, right-sided resection, and presence of unilateral interictal spikes. No evidence was found to suggest that a history of head injury, presence of encephalomalacia, vascular malformations, or postoperative discharges were predictive of outcomes. Multivariable models from 29 studies generally supported the same associations observed in univariate analyses. Variability in the analyses was likely due to small sample sizes, unbalanced group sizes, and differences in the definitions of seizure outcomes and prognostic factors, as well as the influence of surgical site. The authors concluded that limitations in study design and the quality of information presented in the included studies restrict the ability to guide patient selection for surgery and predict surgical outcomes. Future research should prioritize high-quality, prospective studies with adequate statistical power, focusing on specific diagnostic tools, surgical approaches, and the extent of resection. Prognostic factors should be investigated using multivariable regression models, with clinically relevant variables selected for analysis and all numerical results fully reported. Adverse event reporting should be mandatory, and journal editors should reject studies that fail to include this information. The authors emphasized that the stepwise approach used in cancer research, involving well-defined questions and focused RCTs, should be applied to epilepsy surgery to achieve similar advancements.
